paragraphs.text: This essay is about GPT-3, a huge AI program from OpenAI, released in May 2020. GPT-3 is a neural network, a program that learns from examples, with 175 billion adjustable numbers. It learned only by guessing the next word in Internet text.

paragraphs.text: Gwern argues GPT-3 matters because it learned to pick up new tasks from a few examples, though nobody designed it to. He calls this meta-learning, meaning learning how to learn. It supports the "scaling hypothesis": the idea that simple learning programs, made big enough, grow ever more intelligent. GPT-3 was also cheap by government or business standards, so much bigger models are possible.

He argues that predicting human writing well forces a model to learn logic, cause and effect, and reasoning. The last, smallest gains in prediction need the most intelligence.

fuller.text: This long essay by Gwern is about GPT-3, a program released by OpenAI in May 2020 that learned to write by predicting the next word of Internet text. Gwern uses it to argue for the "scaling hypothesis": the idea that making simple neural networks (programs that learn patterns from examples) much bigger makes them smarter.

sentences.text: This long essay by Gwern is about GPT-3, a program released by OpenAI in May 2020 that learned to write by predicting the next word of Internet text.
Gwern uses it to argue for the "scaling hypothesis": the idea that making simple neural networks (programs that learn patterns from examples) much bigger makes them smarter.

fuller.text: GPT-3 was 117 times bigger than GPT-2, yet its gains did not slow down as many expected. Gwern says GPT-3 was cheap by business or government standards, so much larger models are within reach. He notes that old forecasts put the first systems below human level in the 2020s, and says those forecasts are holding up.

fuller.text: The striking new skill is meta-learning: GPT-3 can pick up a new task from a few examples in its prompt, without special training. Gwern's guess is that a big network holds many small sub-models, and with enough data, general rules beat memorized shortcuts. He also argues that predicting human writing well enough forces a model to learn logic, cause and effect, and how people think.

brief.text: This essay looks at GPT-3, a huge computer program that learned to write by reading Internet text. Gwern asks what it shows about how machines become smart. He says it matters because GPT-3 could learn new tasks from just a few examples, which surprised almost everyone.

sentences.text: This essay looks at GPT-3, a huge computer program that learned to write by reading Internet text.
Gwern asks what it shows about how machines become smart.
He says it matters because GPT-3 could learn new tasks from just a few examples, which surprised almost everyone.

brief.text: His key idea is the scaling hypothesis: the claim that simply making these programs bigger makes them smarter. Bigger programs, given more data and computing power, kept getting better with no sign of slowing. He concludes the critics were wrong, and that machines close to human-level may come sooner than experts admit.
